extracted.subtask_description: News coverage of a comedian (Kevin Hart) resigning from a high-profile hosting role after past homophobic tweets resurfaced; the page discusses public apology, institutional responses, and the role of past comedic material. Useful for evaluating how controversies around humor are handled in mainstream media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincere public apology
rubrics_metrics.description: "I sincerely apologize to the LGBTQ community for my insensitive words from my past," — the article reports Hart's apology and later tweets about evolving and loving everybody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece and quoted reactions (e.g., Billy Eichner: "a simple, authentic apology showing any bit of understanding or remorse would have been so simple") indicate that an apology is expected to be authentic, acknowledge harm, and show understanding/remorse; mere words without apparent contrition are criticized. The article contrasts Hart's initial refusal to apologize with the later statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being a distraction as host
rubrics_metrics.description: Hart wrote he withdrew "because I do not want to be a distraction on a night that should be celebrated by so many amazing talented artists."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hosting high-profile events requires avoiding controversy that detracts from the ceremony. If a figure's presence is likely to overshadow the event, stepping down is presented as an appropriate response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional requirement for apology or removal
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Academy of Motion Pictures Arts and Sciences gave him an ultimatum: apologize or 'we're going to have to move on and find another host.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations may demand a public apology or otherwise replace a controversial figure to protect the event/brand. The article frames this as a pragmatic institutional standard applied by the Academy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deleting offensive social media is insufficient once preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hart has since deleted some of the anti-gay tweets... But they had already been screen-captured and been shared online."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that removing posts does not erase their existence or impact; archived/screen-captured material will continue to influence public perception and decisions about suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past comedic material evidences pattern and affects suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes LGBTQ jokes were part of Hart's stand-up (quoting lines like 'one of my biggest fears is my son growing up and being gay' and 'if I can prevent my son from being gay, I will').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic routine content is treated as relevant evidence of attitudes; repeated use of anti-LGBTQ humor contributes to the argument that the comedian's record, not just isolated tweets, is problematic for high-profile roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy-group scrutiny influences outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: "GLAAD... said Thursday that it reached out to Oscars broadcaster ABC, the Academy... to 'discuss Kevin's anti-LGBTQ rhetoric and record.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents advocacy organizations as active monitors that contact institutions to raise concerns; their involvement can spur institutional action or public pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedent matters when evaluating controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece references the 2012 Oscars episode where producer Brett Ratner resigned after using a gay slur and Eddie Murphy subsequently exited; Billy Crystal filled in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past incidents where anti-LGBTQ remarks derailed hosting arrangements are used as precedent to explain institutional and public reactions; history informs expectations about consequences for similar conduct.
